title: Money: A Bible Study on Where Your Treasure Is
subtitle: A five-session study on money, the heart, and the freedom Christ offers.
summary:
This study isn't about the economy. It's about your heart and what it has quietly done with money. Over five sessions we'll look at the heart that follows its treasure, the contentment we keep mistaking for resignation, the rich fool who confused a full barn with a safe soul, the anxiety that drives so much of our reaching, and the freedom of the open hand. It's built so a busy volunteer can lead it without special training. Each question comes with a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer.

It doesn't flatter the generous or scold the greedy, because the line doesn't run between them. It catches the person who gives and still grips, the person who has little and still worships what he lacks, and the giver who has used his giving to stop the question before it reached his heart. None of us stands outside this. Many of us have lain awake doing arithmetic we called prudence, felt our chests loosen at a number in an account and called it peace, and loved our children and let that love become a reason to reach for more. The question isn't whether you may have money. It's what your heart has done with it, and whether, under all the wanting, you can hear the voice of the one who became poor so that you could be free.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: Where Your Treasure Is
sessions.aim: To see that the heart doesn't lead the treasure but follows it, and to stop asking whether money is allowed and start asking where our treasure has already taught our hearts to live.
sessions.summary:
Most of us assume the heart chooses first and the wallet obeys. We love a thing, and then we spend on it. Jesus puts it the other way round: "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also" (Matthew 6:21). The treasure goes first and the heart follows it like a dog on a leash. So the surest way to find out what you love isn't to ask yourself. It's to look at where your money and your worry already go.

This session stays in Matthew 6:19-24: the moth and the rust and the thief, the eye that is the lamp of the body, and the two masters no one can serve. It takes seriously the person who hears all this as guilt about money, and it answers him from the text. Jesus doesn't forbid treasure. He warns against laying it up where it can't last, because the heart goes wherever the treasure is kept. Then he says the thing he won't soften: "You cannot serve God and money" (Matthew 6:24). He doesn't say we shouldn't. He says we can't.

keyScripture.why: "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also" (Matthew 6:21). Jesus reverses the order we assume. Our spending and our worry aren't simply the result of our loves; they're the map of them.

discussion.q: Jesus says, "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also" (Matthew 6:21). He puts the treasure first and the heart second. Before tonight, did you assume your heart leads your money, or that your money leads your heart?
discussion.behind: Find out what people already assume before you teach anything. Most of us assume the heart leads: we love God, and we merely spend on lesser things. Jesus states the order the other way round. You don't need to win the point tonight. Let the room feel how unsettling it is that the treasure trains the heart.

discussion.q: If a stranger studied only your spending and your worry for a month, what would he conclude you love most? Would he be wrong?
discussion.behind: Push past the abstract into evidence. People will defend what they say they love, but this question asks for the trail they've left. The worry is as revealing as the spending, so don't let anyone skip it. You're not hunting for a confession to shame anyone. You want each person, you included, to notice the gap between what we say we treasure and where the leash actually pulls.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 6:19-20 again. Jesus doesn't say "don't lay up treasure." What does he say, and what's true in the worry that this whole subject is just guilt about money?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness early. Jesus tells us to lay up treasure, only somewhere moth and rust and thieves can't reach. The warning isn't against having; it's against storing your heart where it will rot. Make sure no one leaves thinking the answer is to despise provision or feel guilty for owning a house.

discussion.q: "No one can serve two masters" (Matthew 6:24). Where in an ordinary week do you feel the two pulling at you, and which one usually wins without your noticing?
discussion.behind: Make it concrete. The two masters rarely announce a contest. Money tends to win quietly, in the decision made on autopilot and the calendar arranged around earning, while God gets whatever minutes are left. Help people find the moment when the leash tightens and they follow without a thought.

discussion.q: Many of us have loved our children, or someone else we're responsible for, and let that love become a reason to reach for more and never feel it's enough. Where has your treasure pulled your heart somewhere you didn't mean it to go?
discussion.behind: Turn the question on yourself first and answer it briefly and truthfully. You're not after a breakdown, only one real place where your treasure has trained your heart. When the leader goes first, the room usually follows.

objections.objection: This is just shame about money dressed up as theology. Jesus isn't against owning things or saving for the future. His disciples kept a common purse, he ate at rich men's tables, and he never told most of the people he met to get rid of their possessions.
objections.response: Much of that is true, and it matters. Jesus doesn't forbid treasure. He tells us to lay it up, only "in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal" (Matthew 6:20). Provision isn't the sin, and Proverbs praises the ant that stores its food in summer (Proverbs 6:6-8). But there's a distinction here we can't skip. The warning is about location and about the leash. Wherever you put the treasure, the heart goes too, and a heart kept where moths eat is a heart you'll lose without ever deciding to. The question isn't whether you may have money. It's whether your money has quietly come to have you.

objections.objection: I don't think about money that much, so this study is for greedy people, not me. I live simply and I don't chase wealth.
objections.response: Simplicity is a real good, and I won't sneer at it. But notice what not thinking about money can hide. The two masters don't fight loudly in a heart that has already made peace with one of them. The heart can serve money through fear of not having it as surely as through hunger for more, and the anxious, frugal person and the ambitious, reaching person may be bowing to the same master in different postures. Jesus follows his word about two masters straight away with "Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious" (Matthew 6:25). Don't assume that because you aren't greedy you're free. Look at your worry, not only your wanting.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you traced the leash from your heart to your treasure, where would it lead, and is that where you meant your heart to live?
sessions.practice: For three days this week, keep a quiet record of where your money goes and, which is harder, where your worry goes. Don't change anything yet. At the end, read the two lists as a map of what you love, and write down the one place where the map surprised you.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you told us our hearts would follow our treasure, and we've spent years pretending it was the other way round. Show us where we've laid it up, where the moth is already at work, and where our hearts have wandered after it without our permission. We cannot serve you and money both. We've tried, and we're tired. Loosen the leash. Teach us to lay up our treasure with you, so that our hearts can finally come home. In the name of Jesus, the treasure that doesn't rot. Amen.
reflection: If my treasure trains my heart and not the other way round, what has my treasure been quietly teaching my heart to love?
Where have I laid up treasure in a place the moth can reach, and what part of my heart have I lost there without noticing?
When I imagine serving God with my money the way I serve money with my attention, what rises up in me to resist it?
sessions.teaching:
We carry an assumption so deep we hardly ever look at it: the heart leads and the wallet follows. We think we love a thing first and spend on it second, that devotion comes before the dollar. Jesus says the opposite, and I think the reversal ought to stop us. "Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven" (Matthew 6:19-20). Then he gives the reason: "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also" (Matthew 6:21). He puts the treasure first. The heart follows it like a dog on a leash, going where it's pulled. So the surest way to find what you love isn't to search your feelings. It's to follow your money and your worry, because they've already gone ahead to the place your heart will arrive.

Some of us hear this as guilt about money, and that reaction deserves to be taken seriously, because most of us have felt it. It sounds as if Jesus must be against owning, against saving, against the ordinary work of providing for the people you love. But read what he says. He doesn't say "don't lay up treasure." He says don't lay it up here, where moth and rust and thieves can reach it, where everything you store is already wearing away while you stack it. The command isn't to stop treasuring. It's to treasure somewhere loss can't follow. Having isn't the problem. The place is the problem, and it's a serious one, because the heart goes where the treasure is kept, and a heart kept where moths eat is a heart you'll lose without ever choosing to.

Then Jesus says something about the eye that sounds odd to us. "The eye is the lamp of the body. So, if your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light, but if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness" (Matthew 6:22-23). The eye is what you fix your gaze on. In the Jewish idiom Jesus is using, a bad eye, literally an evil eye, is a grudging, grasping eye, the eye that's always doing arithmetic on what it sees. That kind of looking doesn't stay in one corner of a life. You think you're simply being careful, keeping an eye on the numbers, and the keeping of that eye on the numbers is itself the darkness spreading into everything else.

I can't teach this from a safe distance. Most of us have a grasping eye and have called it stewardship. We've lain awake running the figures and called it prudence. I have five sons, and I know how easily providing for them shades into reaching for more, without ever feeling the moment the line was crossed. We love our children and let the love become a reason to reach for more and never enough, and the reaching darkens the very love it claimed to serve.

Then Jesus says it flatly: "No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money" (Matthew 6:24). The word behind "money" is mammon, an Aramaic word, and Jesus speaks of it as if it were a rival lord. He doesn't say we shouldn't serve both. He says we can't, because a heart won't run two ultimate loyalties at once. That isn't a rule so much as a description of how we're made. And what makes money such a cruel master is that it never asks for the contest out loud. It doesn't ask you to renounce God. It only asks for your trust, a little more each year, until you find that the second master has been getting your mornings and your worry and your best attention, and the first has been getting what's left.

This is law before it's grace, and the law has named me. My eye is bad. My treasure has been laid up in the wrong place, and my heart has followed it there. But there's gospel under this, and it's the only thing that loosens the leash. Jesus told a story about a man who found treasure hidden in a field, "then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field" (Matthew 13:44). The kingdom is worth everything, and the king himself made himself poor, down to a borrowed grave, so that our hearts could be kept in him where no moth has ever been. You don't loosen your grip on money to earn him. You loosen it because he has already become the treasure that can't be stolen, and a heart laid up there is safe for the first time.

scriptureStudy.note: "Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal." He doesn't say don't lay up treasure at all. He names a place and the trouble with it: everything stored here is wearing away even while you stack it.
"But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven." The command is still to treasure. Only the address changes. Jesus isn't against storing. He's against storing your heart somewhere it will rot.

"For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." The treasure leads and the heart follows. This one sentence overturns how we think we work, and it makes a bank statement a more truthful confession than many of our prayers.
"The eye is the lamp of the body." What you fix your gaze on fills you with light or with dark. The eye isn't neutral. What it watches runs through the whole of you.

"But if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness." In Jewish idiom a bad or evil eye is a grudging, grasping one. A heart always calculating its gain isn't merely distracted. It's darkening all the way through.
"You cannot serve God and money." Not should not, but cannot. The heart won't run two ultimate loyalties, and money is the master that never asks for the contest out loud.

"For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." Luke sets the same saying right after "Sell your possessions, and give to the needy" (Luke 12:33), which sharpens it. Treasure sent ahead to heaven is the only treasure your heart can safely follow.

The treasure hidden in a field and the pearl of great value. The man sells all he has "in his joy" (Matthew 13:44). It isn't a loss to him. It's the gladdest trade he ever made, because he has found the one treasure worth his whole heart.
